heading: Statistics, with a twist
subheading: Big surprises hide in small numbers. Flip a fact, test your intuition and discover the playful side of statistics.

facts.question: In a room of 23 people, is the chance of a shared birthday above or below 50%?
facts.answer: Just above 50% — about 50.7%! There are 253 pairs to compare. This assumes birthdays are independent and equally likely across 365 days, ignoring leap years.

facts.question: A fair coin lands heads five times in a row. Is tails more likely next?
facts.answer: No — it is still 50/50. Independent coin flips have no memory. Expecting tails to be “due” is called the gambler’s fallacy.

facts.question: One billionaire moves into a small town. Which changes more: mean wealth or median wealth?
facts.answer: The mean can rise dramatically because it includes every value. The median depends on the middle of the ordered values, so it is usually much less affected by a single extreme value.

facts.question: Ice cream sales and sunburns rise together. Does ice cream cause sunburn?
facts.answer: The association alone cannot establish that. Hot, sunny weather can increase both ice cream sales and sun exposure — an example of a possible confounding factor.

facts.question: How many ways can you shuffle a standard 52-card deck?
facts.answer: 52 factorial: about 8.07 × 10⁶⁷ possible orders. That’s a 68-digit number! Every position in the deck multiplies the possibilities.

facts.question: If correlation is zero, does that mean two variables have no relationship?
facts.answer: Not necessarily! Pearson correlation measures linear association. A symmetric U-shaped relationship can have zero correlation even though there is a strong curved pattern.

facts.question: Will a huge online poll always be more accurate than a small random sample?
facts.answer: No. A large sample can still be biased if the people who respond differ systematically from the population. More responses do not automatically fix selection bias.

facts.question: Roll two fair dice. Is a total of 7 more likely than a total of 2?
facts.answer: Yes — six times as likely. Six of the 36 equally likely ordered outcomes total 7; only one, (1, 1), totals 2.
